spec.title: Events in vs rows written (per second)
spec.description: What to look for: k6's accepted rate (202) is the flat line; the consumer's inserted rate drops to 0 when the consumer is killed and shows a catch-up bump above the input rate afterwards. Surprising: a catch-up that never ends (lag keeps growing) or an inserted rate that stays at 0 after the restart. k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so a last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Consumer lag (all partitions)
spec.description: Records in Kafka not yet committed by the group. Grows from the kill until the restarted consumer has joined, then falls to 0. The width of the hump is the time to resume plus the catch-up time. Surprising: lag that does not return to 0 at the end of a run (a partition no one owns).

spec.title: Run phase
spec.description: Added by this experiment (textfile ep_k5_phase, written by run.sh): 0 consumer running, 1 consumer dead, 2 restarted but not processing yet, 3 processing again, -1 no run. Use it to line up every other panel with the kill. Surprising: phase 2 much longer than the session timeout (10 s).

spec.title: Duplicates absorbed by ON CONFLICT (running value)
spec.description: ep_consumer_duplicates_total of the restarted consumer (a counter starts at 0 in every new process, so this is the value of consumer #2 only). In an on-after_db_commit run it jumps once to about the size of the chunk that was in flight when the first consumer died, then stays flat. Always 0 in the other crash points and in the control. With dedup off it stays 0 because nothing checks: the extra rows show up only in the Postgres audit (summary.tsv column dup_rows).

spec.title: Committed offset per partition
spec.description: Last committed offset of the group per partition. Every partition climbs; they all go flat at the kill; after the restart they continue from where they were, not from zero. Surprising: a partition that jumps back (offsets are re-read) or that stays at -1 (never committed).

spec.title: Lag per partition
spec.description: The same gap, split by partition. The partition that was being written when the consumer died is the one whose chunk was handled twice.

spec.title: Partitions owned and group joins
spec.description: Assigned partitions of the running consumer (6 when it owns everything; 0 while it has joined but waits) and the number of assignments it received. After a SIGKILL the old member is only dropped after the session timeout (10 s), so a join of consumer #2 does not give it partitions at once. Surprising: ownership long before 10 s (the broker detected the dead connection).

spec.title: Messages per chunk (mean)
spec.description: Mean size of a chunk the consumer wrote. The chunk in flight at the crash is the number of reprocessed records in the after_db_commit cell, so this is the scale of the duplicates you should expect (the exact number is in the sink log line rows=N and in summary.tsv crash_chunk). A catch-up after the restart uses full chunks (1000).

spec.title: Freshness: API receipt to Postgres commit (p99)
spec.description: How old a row is when it becomes visible. Normally small; it jumps to the length of the outage for the rows that waited, then falls. Only newly inserted rows are measured, never duplicates.

spec.title: Rows inserted in Postgres (per second)
spec.description: Server-side view from the postgres exporter, independent of the consumer's own counters (which vanish with a SIGKILL). With dedup off it also counts the stored-twice rows. Label datname is the database.

spec.title: Consumer process CPU (user and system)
spec.description: CPU seconds per second of the consumer-sink process. It drops to 0 at the kill and shows the catch-up burst after it. Surprising: close to 1 core (the catch-up is CPU-bound on one core).

spec.title: Host CPU busy of the pinned groups
spec.description: Busy share of the CPUs each component is pinned to (variables cpu_server, cpu_consumer, cpu_brokers, cpu_mon). Postgres runs with the monitoring group. Surprising: the consumer or the database CPUs near 100% during the catch-up (then catch-up time is a CPU limit, not a Kafka limit).

spec.title: Database write time (p99) and pool wait
spec.description: p99 of one write transaction of the consumer, and how many callers wait for a pool connection. Surprising: pool waiting above 0 (the consumer runs one partition at a time, so it should stay 0).

spec.title: k6: dropped iterations (must be 0)
spec.description: If k6 could not start every planned request, the number of events sent is below RATE x DURATION and the run is suspect. Must be 0 in every measured run. k6 series are not marked stale after a run.

spec.title: k6: failed requests and latency p99
spec.description: The API is not under test here: failed requests should be 0 and p99 small and flat. Anything else means the producer side is not clean and the audit's acked count is not comparable.

spec.title: k6 CPUs busy (generator headroom)
spec.description: Keep under about 70%. A saturated generator drops iterations and the offered load is not what the label says.

spec.title: Event loop lag p99: API and consumer
spec.description: Node event-loop lag of the ingest-api and of the consumer-sink. Keep under about 50 ms; a blocked loop would delay heartbeats and make the resume time longer than the session timeout.

spec.title: API acknowledged messages (per second)
spec.description: What the API got acknowledged by Kafka (acks=all). It must equal the 202 rate of k6; a gap means events were accepted but not acknowledged.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: did events survive the kill, and how long was the gap?
2. The mechanism: re-delivery after the kill
EventPulse K5 - Kill a consumer at every step
